To: Edwin Van Der Vlist <EdwinVanDerVlist@utdallas.edu>
Cc: Don Proeschel <don.proeschel@utdallas.edu>
Subject: RE: How About a Fall Semester Marketing Project For Exos Aerospace?

Hello Edwin,

Thank you, Don, for the introduction. I would welcome a Fall semester marketing capstone team, and I think we can give your students an unusually good project.

Here is the short version of the client problem. Exos Aerospace is one of only three FAA-licensed reusable rocket launch providers in the United States. We have been flying suborbital vehicles since 2018, and our next flight of BLK3, our precision suborbital reusable launch vehicle, is targeted for early 2027 with roughly 135 kg of payload capacity still open to sell. The capstone challenge is to help us market and sell that payload space.

What makes this different from a normal marketing project is how the team would work. Exos runs an AI-native operating model we call EXO3, an internal fleet of AI agents that already handle research, outreach drafting, and CRM work. The capstone team would sit on top of that stack as the human strategy and creative layer, directing the agents rather than doing all the manual grind themselves. The students learn go-to-market marketing the modern way, humans setting strategy and creative while an agent fleet executes at scale, on a real revenue target. It is a strong story for the business school and, I would think, for your UTDesign showcase.

At a high level a semester could run like this:
- Weeks 1-2: onboard to the EXO3 stack and brand assets, define the ideal payload customer
- Weeks 3-5: segment and size the payload market (university research, defense and government test, in-space startups, sensor and component qualification, education and brand payloads)
- Weeks 5-8: build the campaign, a payload buyer microsite, one-pager, pitch deck, and a social and video series under our SPACEavailable campaign
- Weeks 8-12: run AI-augmented outreach, students author the messaging and creative and the agent fleet personalizes and scales it, all sends approved on our side
- Weeks 12-15: qualify the pipeline, advance the payload manifest for the 2027 flight, and deliver a final presentation and a reusable playbook

We would provide governed access to our tools, brand assets, media, and direct time with me and our BD team. I have put the full project scope in a short brief I can send along once we connect.

Would you have a team available for the fall, and do you have time for a short call this week or next to walk through it? Happy to work around your schedule.

Best regards,

John Quinn
Cofounder & CEO

title: APPROVAL - Reply to Jess Sponable (NFA) with LVES draft charter + template
question: Send this reply to Jess Sponable? On Yes, I deliver the ready-to-send draft (with the LVES charter draft attached) to YOUR inbox for you to send. It does not go to Jess directly.
context:
Jess asked (2026-08-20) for a draft charter / draft contents and a committee-charter template in the proper format. Draft charter built (drafts/LVES_Charter_DRAFT_v0.1_2026-08-20.md, attached to MC task 2169) in standard AIAA TC format, expanding the current LVES scope per Jess's takes (ELV+RLV, reusable upper stages/SM&L/ISAM/refueling, hypersonic suborbital in-core, hypersonic aircraft as interfaces, operability/reliability/safety cross-cutting). Reply answers both her questions and engages each scope point.

----- DRAFT REPLY -----
To: Jess Sponable <jess@nfaero.com>
Subject: RE: LVES Charter Working Group - Action

Hello Jess,

Good instincts on all of it, and yes, I have something concrete. I put together a first draft of the charter plus the contents we should include, and I built it in the standard AIAA TC format so it drops straight into the working group. Draft is attached.

On your two questions:

1. Draft charter / draft of contents: attached as a v0.1. It builds on the current LVES TC scope we already have and expands it along the lines you raised, rather than starting from a blank page.

2. Template in the proper format: because LVES is already an AIAA Technical Committee, the AIAA TC charter is the format, Committee Name, Scope, Governance, Roles and Responsibilities, with a versioned header and an annual review. If you want clean sister examples in that exact format, the AIAA Adaptive Structures and Transformational Flight charters are both public on aiaa.org, and the AIAA TAD Policy and Procedures points to a sample charter in the TC Chair Handbook. I patterned the draft on those.

On your scope takes, here is how I handled each in the draft:

- ELVs and RLVs: core, full vehicle systems and operations.
- Upper stages stepping to reusable upper stages: core, with SM&L, ISAM, refueling, and dynamic maneuver named as the enabling technologies, so we interface to that future without pretending we own the whole in-space architecture.
- Hypersonic suborbital rockets: in core, since they share vehicle, propulsion integration, GNC, thermal, and operations technology with launch and entry.
- Rocket-powered and airbreathing hypersonic aircraft: named as interfaces rather than absorbed. The common-technology argument is real, which is exactly why I kept them as coordinated interfaces, so we capture the shared tech without losing the constraint or stepping on the hypersonics committees.
- Operability, reliability, and safety of RLVs and ELVs: made a standing cross-cutting theme, since that is the connective tissue across every concept on the list.

I also added explicit exclusions, because constraining the problem matters as much as defining it, and one governance item: an objectives ledger baked into the charter from day one, every objective with an owner, a deliverable, a due date, and a quarterly status, so this committee produces named sessions and a roadmap rather than another round of minutes. Happy to stand that up and maintain it for the group.

Take a red pen to it. I would rather hand John Vinson a marked-up draft than more open discussion.

Best,
John

title: Send reply to Anselmo Pontes (Autogenetics) — GA/evolutionary trajectory-optimization brief
question: Approve sending this reply to Anselmo Pontes (Autogenetics) with the specific-problems write-up he requested, then a meeting in the next two weeks? Edit freely before sending.
context:
John reached out after Anselmo's HelioTech talk; Anselmo replied warmly (8/31, CC Neil Milburn) asking for a brief description of the specific trajectory problems before meeting. Draft reply below.

----- DRAFT (To: anselmo@autogenetics.ai; Cc: nmilburn@exosaero.com) -----
Subject: RE: Anselmo Pontes (Autogenetics) — evolutionary algorithms / trajectory convergence

Hello Anselmo,

Thank you, it was a genuine pleasure comparing notes, and I appreciate you offering to dig into the trajectory side with me. Here is the brief you asked for.

The core question I want your read on: do evolutionary/genetic methods converge more robustly, and toward better global optima, than the gradient-based approaches (direct collocation / pseudospectral transcription solved with SQP) we typically reach for on these problems? Ours are non-convex, heavily constrained, and often multi-objective, exactly the regime where gradient methods get pinned to a local optimum or stall on a poor initial guess.

The specific problems I have in mind, all on a reusable suborbital vehicle (our BLK3):

1. Powered-descent / propulsive-landing guidance. Converging on fuel-optimal descent-and-landing trajectories under thrust, thermal, and structural-load constraints, with tight terminal precision at the pad.

2. Ascent optimization. Pitch and throttle program to hit a target apogee/altitude with minimum propellant while staying inside our load limits (nominal boost under ~4g, transients to ~7g).

3. Coast and apogee targeting, plus contingency/abort trajectories off nominal.

Where I would most value your view: whether an evolutionary method, possibly hybridized with a local refinement step, converges more reliably across this set than what we use today, where you have seen it work well, and where it does not. If there is a fit, a natural extension is coupling the trajectory to vehicle-configuration/aero geometry, which is closer to the free-molecular-flow work you presented.

The easiest way to find a time in the next couple of weeks is to book directly on my calendar here, and I will hold Tuesdays and Thursdays open since those work best for you:
https://outlook.office365.us/bookwithme/user/3d1b68ea7e5643f9b2e76624f9dfd95f%40exosaero.com?anonymous&ismsaljsauthenabled

Best Regards,
John
